By checking the convergence of individual variables and comparing to reference quantities that are
meaningful even when the solution is not changing, `ReferenceResidualProblem` addresses the first two
issues listed above. The third issue is potentially more of a problem with `ReferenceResidualProblem`
than the standard MOOSE convergence check, and dealing with
it is discussed in [#zero_resid].

Use of this procedure requires that the user provide physically meaningful reference quantities. The
vector of the reaction loads (in the case of mechanics) or integrated fluxes (in the case of
diffusion problems) is typically suitable for this purpose, as it provides a measure of the loading
applied to the system. To make these reference quantities, simply add the
[!param](/Kernels/NullKernel/extra_vector_tags) parameter to the computing objects that you
want to add into the reference vector. An explicit example is given in [#example] below.
Alternatively, the [!param](/Kernels/NullKernel/absolute_value_vector_tags)` parameter can be
used in the kernels to assemble the absolute value of the contribution to each degree of freedom
affected by the kernel.

Since relative convergence is computed differently with this approach, the nonlinear relative
tolerance required to achieve the same error is typically different than with the default approach in
MOOSE, and the differences will vary by the problem. The code user must evaluate the behavior of
their model to ensure that appropriate tolerances are being used.

### Dealing with Residuals that are Zero at Boundaries id=zero_resid

As mentioned in the third case above where relative convergence checks can fail,
the converged solutions for some problems are zero on all boundaries with Dirichlet
boundary condition (BC) because of the nature of the loading conditions. This would
make the `ReferenceResidualProblem` convergence checks fail because the norm of the
reference vector would be zero in this case.  This is manifested when the reference
values decrease at the same rate as the residuals, so relative convergence is never
achieved.

In some mechanics problems, such as those with symmetry planes, this might happen
only in one direction. This situation can be remedied by grouping together the
residuals for all components of the displacement variables rather than checking
them individually. If the reference vector for one of the variables in the group
is zero (because there are no Dirichlet BCs that restrict the solution in that direction),
but it is nonzero for the others, the residual for the set of variables will
be checked together, and the variable with a zero value will not prevent
convergence as it normally would.  Grouping variables is accomplished by
using the `group_variables` option, which is used to provide one or more
lists of names of variables to group together.

In some cases, however, there may be no degrees of freedom with nonzero residuals
at Dirichlet BCs for even a group of variables.  This could happen in mechanics
problems that only have free expansion, in which the Dirichlet BCs are important
for preventing rigid body motion, but do not restrain the deformation of the body.
This could also happen if there is simply no loading on a model during a time step.

It is necessary in such cases to also specify an absolute tolerance using `nl_abs_tol`,
which is a problem-specific value that must be higher than the residual below which
the solution can no longer converge tighter due to numeric roundoff errors, but sufficiently
low to ensure that the solution is converged when that limit is reached.

Alternatively, the [!param](/Kernels/NullKernel/absolute_value_vector_tags)
parameter can be used in the kernels or the action that sets them up. This option does not
rely on the use of Dirichlet BCs to compute a meaningful reference vector, and can typically
remedy this issue.

content.content:
val-2d_csvdiff fails at dtmin with PETSc 3.26
CLOSED
## Bug Description
With PETSc 3.26 (MOOSE package update idaholab/moose#33833), `val-2d_csvdiff` aborts with `Solve failed and timestep already at dtmin, cannot continue!`.

PETSc 3.26 keeps a user-provided convergence test for `vinewtonrsls`, so MOOSE's `ReferenceResidualConvergence` now decides convergence of val-2d's variational inequality solves instead of PETSc's `SNESConvergedDefault_VI`. MOOSE's check compares each variable's residual against its own reference residual. val-2d sets `nl_rel_tol = 1e-10` with no absolute tolerance (the default is 1e-50). Where `trapped_1`'s reference residual is small (about 7e-2 at t ~ 28 s), that relative target is below the round-off floor of the converged residual. Newton then stagnates near 1e-11 and the time step is cut back to dtmin.

A separate defect in the same path, residual entries at nodes held at a bound being included in the reference residual norms, is fixed in idaholab/moose#33833. That fix gets val-2d past its first time step; this issue covers the remaining tolerance problem.

## Steps to Reproduce
Build TMAP8 against idaholab/moose#33833 (PETSc 3.26) and run `./run_tests --re val-2d.val-2d_csvdiff`. The solve stagnates at time step 16 (t ~ 28 s) and the step is cut back to dtmin. CI shows the same failure in the Conda External App tests and Apptainer rocky8-gcc-openmpi public apps jobs on that PR.

## Impact
Blocks the MOOSE package update (idaholab/moose#33833): the TMAP8 jobs on that PR fail. Adding `Executioner/nl_abs_tol=1e-9` to the val-2d test arguments lets the solves converge with PETSc 3.26. With PETSc 3.25 it leaves the output unchanged from the current gold in serial, two processes, and debug builds, so no regold is needed.

content.text:
I reproduced all six CI failures locally and fixed val-2d. val-2g still fails: the fix I tried for it needs a regold and slows one test into a timeout, so I reverted it and need your decision on how to proceed. Nothing is committed yet.

**What broke.** The failing `Test heavy` job was not caused by the MOOSE bump in `988daaa1`. The same six tests first failed at `2d31c413`, the submodule bump that brought in PETSc 3.26; `268bf685` passed. Under PETSc 3.26, MOOSE's `ReferenceResidualConvergence` decides when `vinewtonrsls` solves have converged, which is the cause behind issue #476. PR #477 fixed only the light val-2d tests, through `cli_args`. The heavy val-2d test and all of val-2g kept no usable absolute tolerance.

**How I reproduced it.** I built TMAP8 against the `moose` submodule with `METHOD=opt` and 64 jobs, as you asked, rather than the `cuda-mpich-moose` path in my saved notes. Your shell sets `METHOD=dbg`, so I had to set it explicitly. Old opt libraries in the tree still pointed at `/opt/openmpi` and broke the link, so I deleted them. Running `./run_tests --heavy --pedantic-checks --re 'val-2(d|g)'` then gave the same six failures as CI.

**val-2d (fixed, not committed).** I moved `nl_abs_tol = 1e-9` from the light tests' `cli_args` into `val-2d.i`, so the light tests, the heavy test and the documented input all use it. All val-2d tests now pass against the existing gold files, with no regold.

**val-2g (still failing).** In every failing step, one variable's residual stops falling at about 2.0e-6:
- `Oxygen_vacancy_concentration_dry` has a reference residual of only about 1.8e-3.
- With `nl_rel_tol = 1e-7`, it would need to reach about 1.8e-10.
- That is far below the round-off floor. The wet vacancy residual stops at the same 2.03e-6, which fits a floor set by the vacancy concentration's size (about 6.5e8 at/µm³).

Newton reaches that floor in 3–4 iterations, then bounces between two values until `nl_max_its = 10` and the time step is cut down to dtmin. These are the tolerance changes I tried:

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| Reference vector from `absolute_value_vector_tags` | Still stops at dtmin |
| `nl_abs_tol = 1e-8` or `1e-6` | Still stops at dtmin (1e-6 is below the 2e-6 floor) |
| `nl_abs_tol = 1e-5` | Solves finish and `pss_optimization` passes. Two CSV tests differ from gold (`recombination_flux_T2_wet_left` by 22% in the first output row, everything else 1e-5 or less). `trapping_calibrated_csv` times out because dt falls to about 4e-4. |

Changing val-2g's tolerance and regolding is a physics modelling decision, so I want your call before going further. The options I see:
1. Use `nl_abs_tol = 1e-5`, regold the two CSV tests, and look into the `trapping_calibrated` slowdown.
2. Keep the solver tolerance tight but stop the near-static dry vacancy variable from setting its own relative target, for example by grouping variables with `group_variables`. I haven't tested this yet.
3. Something you prefer.

I also need the TMAP8 issue number for the commits. I can reuse #476, which is closed, or open a new bug-report issue.

content.content:
Add left and right diagonal scaling to SNES and TS
opened lindad 2026-08-05T04:26:51.704Z
This MR adds left and right diagonal scaling to `SNES`, and through its stage solves to `TS`:

- `SNESSetDiagonalScale(snes, func, ctx)` sets a `SNESDiagonalScaleFn` that fills the left and right scale vectors. `DMSNESSetDiagonalScale()` and `DMSNESGetDiagonalScale()` are the `DMSNES` versions.
- `DMSNESSetFieldDiagonalScales(dm, nfields, left[], right[])` installs a callback that gives each entry the value of its field, from `DMCreateFieldDecomposition()`.
- `SNESComputeDiagonalScale()` calls the callback. `SNESDiagonalScaleToPhysical()` and `SNESDiagonalScaleToSolver()` convert vectors for user monitors and convergence tests.
- petsc4py: `SNES.setDiagonalScale()` and `DM.setSNESFieldDiagonalScales()`/`getSNESFieldDiagonalScales()`.

With a left scale $L$ and a right scale $R$, `SNES` solves $L\,F(R y) = L\,b$ for $y$ and returns $x = R y$. $R$ is a change of variables, and each of its entries is a typical magnitude of an unknown. $L$ weights the equations, and each of its entries is the inverse of a typical residual magnitude. Thus this is nondimensionalization at the solver interface. The scaled problem has the same root as the unscaled problem. `diagonal-scaling-math.md` (branch `lindad/diagonal-scaling-math-doc`) gives the full mathematical definition.

## Motivation

In Lagrange-multiplier mechanical contact, $J_{dd}$ (displacement) is of the order of Young's modulus, $O(10^9)$ to $O(10^{12})$, while $J_{d\lambda}$ is of geometric order, approximately $O(1)$. MOOSE already applies a left scale per physics, but a left scale cannot correct this. The fix is a change of variables. Users can nondimensionalize by hand, but that is error-prone. MOOSE can compute a good right scale automatically, so it needs PETSc to apply it.

## Design

The scaling lives in `SNES`, and `KSP` does not know about it.

1. **Conversion only at the interface.** Each user callback that defines the problem (function, Jacobian, objective, NGS, `SNESNEWTONAL` tangent load) gets and returns physical values. `SNESComputeJacobian()` replaces an assembled user Jacobian with $L J R$ through `MatDiagonalScale()`. `SNESSolve()` converts the solution, the right-hand side, and the variable bounds on entry and on exit.
2. **No conversion two times.** PETSc callbacks that difference `SNESComputeFunction()` or `SNESComputeObjective()` are already in solver units. Examples are `-snes_fd`, `-snes_fd_color`, `-snes_mf`, `-snes_mf_operator`, Galerkin FAS, and the secant NGS. They get no conversion, and their matrices are not scaled.
3. **A nested solver uses the space of its parent.** A nonlinear preconditioner, a `SNESCOMPOSITE` sub-solver, and a `SNESFAS` smoother share the parent's scale vectors. These solvers, `SNESFAS` coarse levels, and `SNESNASM` subdomain solvers get solver-unit vectors and do no conversion of their own.

**The scales are part of the problem definition, like $F$.** The callback is stored in the `DMSNES`, which `DMCoarsen()`, `DMRefine()`, and `DMCreateDomainDecomposition()` pass to each new `DM`. Each `SNES` calls the callback at setup on its own `DM`. Thus `SNESFAS` coarse levels, rediscretized `PCMG` levels, `SNESNASM` subdomains, and grid-sequenced levels get scales in their own layout, and no scale vector is restricted or scattered. The callback fills vectors and does not apply an operator, because `SNES` needs the diagonals for `MatDiagonalScale()`, for variable bounds, and for the objective check. `SNES` does not query the `DM` itself. Only `DMSNESSetFieldDiagonalScales()` uses the field decomposition. Per-field scales are exact on coarse levels, because they commute with transfer operators that do not mix fields. For scales that change inside a field, the FAS tau correction keeps the coarse problem consistent, so the coarse scales change only the efficiency.

User line-search and trust-region pre-checks and post-checks get the physical iterate, step, and candidate. A step or candidate that they change is converted back to solver units. Monitors and convergence tests get the solver norms, because the norm of a residual with mixed units has no clear meaning. Thus all `SNES` and `KSP` tolerances are in solver units. With $\ell_i$ equal to the inverse of a typical residual of equation $i$, `-snes_atol` is a per-equation physical tolerance of $\mathrm{atol}/\ell_i$.

With an objective, $L$ and $R$ must be equal, so that the objective stays a potential for the scaled residual. Each entry of each scale must be positive. `SNESComputeDiagonalScale()` checks this. `SNESPATCH` is not supported. It fails without scaling on the DMPlex problems we tried, and that work belongs in a separate MR.

For `TS`, the user sets the callback on the `SNES` from `TSGetSNES()`. `TSSetUp()` sets `vatol = atol * R` when the user has not set a `vatol`, so the absolute part of the error control has the units of the state. Sensitivity analysis (`TSAdjoint`, `TSForward`) uses the physical Jacobian, so sensitivities do not depend on the scales. When the user gives only a RHS Jacobian, `TS` gives the `SNES` its own Jacobian matrices while scales are set. This keeps the kept RHS Jacobian in physical units for the paths that reuse it.

content.text:
**On the best choice:** a single `nl_abs_tol` is the weakest part of option 1. The better fix is a convergence floor that scales with each variable's own magnitude. Option 1 is still a reasonable stopgap if one check passes first.

**Why the solve stalls.** `automatic_scaling` makes the Jacobian diagonal about 1, so each scaled residual is measured in the units of its own variable. Its round-off floor is then about eps × ‖x_i‖:
- `Oxygen_vacancy_concentration` is about 0.05·N ≈ 6.5e8 on about 600 nodes.
- That gives 2.2e-16 × 6.5e8 × √600 ≈ 3.5e-6, which matches the observed 2.0–3.0e-6 for both the dry and wet copies.
- The electron floor estimate (about 3e-10) is within an order of magnitude of the observed 6e-11.

The variables differ in size by many orders of magnitude, so one absolute tolerance cannot suit them all. An `nl_abs_tol` of 1e-5 clears the vacancy floor by only 3–5×, so CI hardware could still hit it. It also sits about 5 orders above the floors of the electron and OT variables. A looser solve there may explain the 22% change in `recombination_flux_T2_wet_left` in the first output row.

Before regolding with option 1, I would check that the outputs barely change when `nl_abs_tol` varies from about 5e-6 to 1e-4. If they hold steady, the accepted solutions are converged where it matters. I can't yet say whether the new numbers or the gold are closer to the truth. The gold came from PETSc 3.25's own VI test, which measures one global norm dominated by the largest variables, so it may also be under-converged in the small ones.

The `trapping_calibrated_csv` timeout is probably my fault. I ran it while other heavy runs were using the same cores, so it needs a run on its own before I treat it as real.

**On the variables, and MR 9476:**
- val-2g has 8 nonlinear variables: `OT_concentration`, `Oxygen_vacancy_concentration`, `electron_concentration` and `trapped_1`, each as a dry and a wet copy. The physics is diffusion of the three mobile species, trapping and release of OT, and surface reactions in the boundary-condition materials. The dry and wet cases share no nonlinear coupling.
- Yes, MR 9476 targets exactly this. With a right scale R_i set to each variable's typical size, the floor becomes about eps·√n for every variable. One solver-unit tolerance then means the same thing for all 8 variables, and the MR's per-equation tolerance (atol/ℓ_i) gives the per-variable floors this problem needs.
- The benefit is in the tolerance, not in conditioning. The linear solves already reach about 1e-21 with LU, so better conditioning would not help here.
- Two caveats:
  - The relative check `res/ref` does not change under per-field scaling, so only the absolute part improves.
  - `ReferenceResidualConvergence` computes its own norms from MOOSE's residual vector. It would have to convert them to solver units, for example with `SNESDiagonalScaleToSolver()`.
- The MR is still open, so it can't fix CI now.

**My proposal:**
1. Run the tolerance check above.
2. If the outputs are stable, use option 1 with a tolerance of about 3e-5, roughly 10× the floor, rather than 1e-5. Then regold.
3. Rerun `trapping_calibrated_csv` by itself to see whether it really times out.
4. Note in the commit that a per-variable floor, through MR 9476 or a MOOSE per-variable absolute tolerance, is the principled replacement.

I still need the issue number for the commits: reuse #476 (closed) or open a new one.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Compare CSV postprocessor files column by column.

Usage: csvcmp.py REF.csv OTHER.csv [OTHER.csv ...]

For each OTHER file, prints the columns whose largest difference from REF exceeds
--floor relative to that column's peak magnitude, as max |diff| / peak.
"""
import argparse
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("ref")
parser.add_argument("others", nargs="+")
parser.add_argument("--floor", type=float, default=1e-6)
parser.add_argument("--columns", nargs="*", default=None)
args = parser.parse_args()

ref = pd.read_csv(args.ref)
for path in args.others:
    other = pd.read_csv(path)
    n = min(len(ref), len(other))
    print(f"== {path}  rows ref/other {len(ref)}/{len(other)}")
    if not np.allclose(ref["time"].values[:n], other["time"].values[:n], rtol=1e-12, atol=0):
        print("   time columns differ; comparing row by row anyway")
    cols = args.columns if args.columns else [c for c in ref.columns if c != "time"]
    for c in cols:
        if c not in other:
            print(f"   {c}: missing")
            continue
        x = ref[c].values[:n]
        y = other[c].values[:n]
        peak = np.abs(x).max()
        if peak == 0:
            continue
        d = np.abs(x - y)
        rel = d.max() / peak
        if rel > args.floor:
            i = int(d.argmax())
            print(f"   {c:42s} {rel:.2e}  at row {i} t={ref['time'].values[i]:.4g}"
                  f"  ref={x[i]:.6e} other={y[i]:.6e}")

vinewtonrsls solves and checks each variable against its own reference
residual. The scaled residual of a variable cannot drop below about

electron_concentration_dry stalls near 4e-5 during desorption in the
calibrated case. An nl_abs_tol of 3e-4 clears both floors. Outputs

All six heavy-test failures from the CI job are fixed locally on branch `fix-heavy-val-2d-2g`. All 7 heavy tests in val-2d and val-2g pass, and so do the light tests and the comparison scripts. I haven't pushed anything or opened a PR.

**One change from my proposal:** I set val-2g's `nl_abs_tol` to **3e-4**, not the 3e-5 I suggested.
- The sweep showed that `trapping_calibrated` stalls on a second variable. During desorption (t ≈ 9100 s), `electron_concentration_dry` stops falling at 3.2–4.3e-5, while its reference residual is only 7.6e-2.
- So 3e-5 and every smaller value I tried still cut the time step down to dtmin.
- This also means I guessed wrong earlier: the `trapping_calibrated` timeout was a real stall, not my overloaded machine.
- The floor that matters moves from one variable to another during the run. That is more evidence that a per-variable tolerance, such as MR 9476 would give, is the principled fix.

**The tolerance check:**
- With `nl_abs_tol` between 1e-4 and 1e-3, every output changes by less than about 2e-3 relative, and most by less than 1e-4.
- Against the old gold, the differences are below 3e-3 everywhere except the first output step. There, `recombination_flux_T2_wet_left` in the no-trapping case moves by 22%. The new value is the same at 1e-4, 3e-4 and 1e-3, so the old gold was the less converged answer.
- Run times are unchanged at about 90–125 s.

**The commits**, each referencing #476 and including the session `.jsonl`:
1. `78608219` moves `nl_abs_tol = 1e-9` from the light val-2d tests' `cli_args` into `val-2d.i`. The output matches the existing gold, so no regold was needed.
2. `c28973cb` sets val-2g's `nl_abs_tol = 3e-4`. Following the project rule, it records the resulting CSVDiff failures in its message.
3. `de2b901f` regolds the three heavy val-2g CSV files.

I left the untracked `test/tests/val-2f/*.prof` files alone. Should I push the branch and open a draft PR?

- So it seems like a better computer-science/math design would be to add the option to specify per-physics/variable absolute tolerances in ReferenceResidualInterface/Convergence?
- So we started converging more tightly after the PETSc update in val-2g, e.g. because we started honoring the ReferenceResidualConvergence?

content.text:
**1. Per-variable absolute tolerances.** Yes, that is the better design. It gives each variable a convergence floor that fits its own magnitude. `nl_abs_tol` is a single number compared against every variable's residual. The variables differ by many orders of magnitude, so any single value is either below some variable's round-off floor or far too loose for another.

There are two ways to build it in `ReferenceResidualInterface`/`ReferenceResidualConvergence`:

- **Explicit per-variable or per-group absolute tolerances.** This would be a vector parameter that matches `group_variables`/`converge_on`. It is simple and fits MOOSE's style. The weakness shows in val-2g: the variable at its floor changes during the run. `Oxygen_vacancy_concentration` stalls near 2e-6 at the start of charging. `electron_concentration_dry` stalls near 4e-5 during desorption. A fixed value per variable must cover that variable's worst moment over the whole run.
- **An automatic floor.** This would be a tolerance proportional to machine epsilon times a measure of each variable's size, recomputed every solve. It needs no tuning and follows changes in time. The catch is that the electron floor during desorption is far above my magnitude-only estimate for that variable. So the floor seems to depend on conditioning as well as on the solution's size. I would have to show that a cheap measure, such as ‖x_i‖ or the diagonal of the Jacobian block, predicts the floor before trusting it.

My recommendation is the explicit version first, possibly with the automatic floor as an option later. This is a change to MOOSE's public interface, so I'd want your go-ahead before writing it. MR 9476 is the PETSc-level version of the same idea: with a right scale for each field, one solver-unit tolerance means the same thing for every variable.

**2. Did we start converging more tightly?** Most likely yes, for the small variables. It follows from MOOSE's convergence check now actually being used.

- Before PETSc 3.26, PETSc replaced MOOSE's convergence test for `vinewtonrsls` with its own `SNESConvergedDefault_VI`. That test measures one global norm over the inactive set, dominated by the largest variables.
- With `nl_rel_tol = 1e-7` against an initial ‖R‖ of about 2.8e10 at the first step, that test accepted a global residual of about 3e3. Variables whose residuals are around 1e-3 to 1e2 were not really being checked.
- Now each variable must meet 1e-7 times its own reference residual, or the 3e-4 absolute tolerance. For the small variables that is far tighter than before.

The data supports this. The new outputs agree to about 2e-3 or better across `nl_abs_tol` from 1e-4 to 1e-3. The old gold differs most where small, early quantities matter: the 22% change in `recombination_flux_T2_wet_left` at the first output step. The gold was the less converged answer.

Two caveats:
- I worked out the old acceptance threshold from MOOSE's tolerances and PETSc's documented VI test. I didn't run against a PETSc 3.25 build to watch it happen.
- The same mechanism caused the original dtmin failures. Under the global test, a variable sitting at its round-off floor never blocked convergence. Under the per-variable test, it does.

# A negative source drives u below its lower bound of zero over part of the domain, so the
# variational inequality solver holds those degrees of freedom at the bound, where the residual
# stays nonzero. The reference residual convergence check must exclude them to converge.

[Mesh]
  type = GeneratedMesh
  dim = 1
  nx = 20
[]

[Problem]
  type = ReferenceResidualProblem
  extra_tag_vectors = 'ref'
  reference_vector = 'ref'
[]

[Variables]
  [u]
  []
[]

[AuxVariables]
  [bounds_dummy]
  []
[]

[Kernels]
  [diff]
    type = Diffusion
    variable = u
    extra_vector_tags = 'ref'
  []
  [source]
    type = BodyForce
    variable = u
    value = -10
    extra_vector_tags = 'ref'
  []
[]

[BCs]
  [left]
    type = DirichletBC
    variable = u
    boundary = left
    value = 1
  []
  [right]
    type = DirichletBC
    variable = u
    boundary = right
    value = 0
  []
[]

[Bounds]
  [u_lower_bound]
    type = ConstantBounds
    variable = bounds_dummy
    bounded_variable = u
    bound_type = lower
    bound_value = 0
  []
[]

[Executioner]
  type = Steady
  solve_type = NEWTON
  petsc_options_iname = '-pc_type -snes_type'
  petsc_options_value = 'lu vinewtonrsls'
  nl_rel_tol = 1e-10
  nl_abs_tol = 1e-50
  nl_max_its = 20
[]

[Outputs]
  exodus = true
[]
50-  []
51-

53-    type = 'Exodiff'
54:    input = 'reference_residual_active_bounds.i'

59-  []
60-
61-  [exceptions]
62-    requirement = "The system shall"
63-    issues = '#14946'
64-    design = 'ConstantBounds.md'
65-    [solver]

# ReferenceResidualConvergence

This [Convergence](Convergence/index.md) is a [/DefaultNonlinearConvergence.md] with a
customized reference residual for its relative convergence checks. See
[ReferenceResidualProblem.md] for more information.

With a variational inequality solver (`-snes_type vinewtonrsls` or `vinewtonssls`, used with
[Bounds](Bounds/index.md)), the residual at degrees of freedom held at a bound (the active set) is
excluded from the residual norms, since the bound constraint holds there in place of the residual
equation.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Estimate per-variable residual floors from a MOOSE reference residual console log.

Usage: floors.py LOG [LOG ...]

A solve's final iterations stall at the round-off floor. For each nonlinear solve, the
residual of each variable at its last two iterations bounds that floor. This prints, per
variable, quantiles over solves of max(res at last two iterations).
"""
import re
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

import numpy as np

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""List the variables that block convergence in failed nonlinear solves of a MOOSE log.
3	
4	Usage: blockers.py ABS_TOL REL_TOL LOG [LOG ...]
5	
6	For each solve that ends in "Solve Did NOT Converge", reads the per-variable residuals
7	at its last iteration and reports the variables that fail both the absolute and the
8	relative check. Only solves whose blocking residual stagnated (changed by less than a
9	factor of 10 over the last three iterations) count, which excludes solves that diverged.
10	Prints, per blocking variable, the count and the range of residuals.
11	"""
12	import re
13	import sys
14	from collections import defaultdict
15	
16	ansi = re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m")
17	var_line = re.compile(r"^\s+(\S+)-> res: (\S+)\s+ref: (\S+)")
18	
19	abs_tol = float(sys.argv[1])
20	rel_tol = float(sys.argv[2])
21	blocked = defaultdict(list)
22	for path in sys.argv[3:]:
23	    iters = []
24	    current = {}
25	    with open(path, errors="replace") as f:
26	        for raw in f:
27	            line = ansi.sub("", raw)
28	            m = var_line.match(line)
29	            if m:
30	                current[m.group(1)] = (float(m.group(2)), float(m.group(3)))
31	                continue
32	            if "Nonlinear |R|" in line and current:
33	                iters.append(current)
34	                current = {}
35	            elif "Solve Did NOT Converge" in line:
36	                if len(iters) >= 3:
37	                    for v, (res, ref) in iters[-1].items():
38	                        hist = [it[v][0] for it in iters[-3:] if v in it]
39	                        stagnant = len(hist) == 3 and max(hist) < 10 * max(min(hist), 1e-300)
40	                        if stagnant and res >= abs_tol and res >= rel_tol * ref:
41	                            blocked[v].append(res)
42	                iters = []
43	
44	for v in sorted(blocked):
45	    r = sorted(blocked[v])
46	    print(f"{v:36s} solves {len(r):5d} res min {r[0]:.2e} median {r[len(r)//2]:.2e} max {r[-1]:.2e}")

A residual cannot drop below a round-off floor that scales with its

residual of others. The Newton solve then stagnates, or it accepts an
unconverged result.

tolerances. These replace nl_abs_tol for those variables. Variables in a
group of group_variables must share one tolerance, because the check
uses one residual norm for each group. The acceptable_multiplier applies
to these tolerances also.

content.text:
I added a per-variable absolute tolerance, `variable_nl_abs_tol`, to `ReferenceResidualConvergence` and `ReferenceResidualProblem`, and switched val-2g to use it. Nothing is pushed.

**MOOSE** (commit `05c7f115938` on local branch `ref-resid-var-abs-tol`, based on the current submodule commit):
- **Syntax:** `variable_nl_abs_tol` pairs variable names with tolerances, e.g. `'u 1e-4 v 1e-8'`. Unlisted variables keep `nl_abs_tol`. All variables in a `group_variables` group must have the same tolerance, because a group is checked against a single residual norm. `acceptable_multiplier` scales these tolerances too, and the console colors use them.
- **Errors:** the input is rejected if it names an unknown variable, gives a negative tolerance, or gives a group's variables different tolerances.
- **Framework test** `variable_abs_tol.i`: two decoupled variables whose residuals differ by 1e8. It converges with a per-variable tolerance and fails with any single `nl_abs_tol`. More cases cover the acceptable multiplier and the three errors.
- **Docs:** a new section in `ReferenceResidualConvergence.md`.
- **Results:** the full framework test suite passes (5636 tests, 0 failed). The reference-residual, bounds and convergence tests also pass with `-p 2` and with `--distributed-mesh`. The contact module's AL tests pass; that module builds on this class.

**TMAP8** (on branch `val-2g-variable-abs-tol`, which builds on the earlier `fix-heavy-val-2d-2g` commits):
- `1079e594` points the `moose` submodule at the new commit and sets per-variable tolerances in `val-2g_trapping.i`:
  - `Oxygen_vacancy_concentration_dry`/`_wet`: 3e-5
  - `electron_concentration_dry`: 3e-4
  - `electron_concentration_wet`: 1e-5

  The default `nl_abs_tol` drops from 3e-4 to 1e-6, so the other four variables are now converged 300× more tightly. The commit message records the CSVDiff failures.
- `920e39d2` regolds the three heavy CSV files. Values moved less than 1e-4 relative from the 3e-4 gold.
- All 7 heavy val-2d/val-2g tests pass, including the PSS optimization that uses `val-2g_trapping.i`. The light tests pass too. Run times are about 100–130 s, roughly what they were.

**Before this can merge:**
- The submodule bump points at a commit that exists only in my local checkout, so TMAP8 CI can't fetch it. The MOOSE PR has to merge first, and then the TMAP8 change needs a normal submodule update.
- The two TMAP8 branches share history. You could merge `fix-heavy-val-2d-2g` alone as a stopgap, since it needs no MOOSE change, and follow it with this branch.
- The MOOSE commit references #33833. Open a MOOSE issue first if you want a dedicated one.

Shall I push both branches and open draft PRs?

**Answers to your questions**

1. **Absolute tolerance and solution size.** You're right that the tolerance is compared against the residual, not the solution. My wording was loose. The floor is still set by the solution, though, because the residual is computed from it. Each solution entry carries rounding error of about eps·|x|, and the Jacobian turns that into residual noise of about eps·‖J_i‖·‖x_i‖. With `automatic_scaling`, ‖J_i‖ is about 1, so the floor looks like eps·‖x_i‖. That explains the vacancy floor. Two more effects can raise the floor:
   - Residuals built as a small difference of large terms. The reaction flux in `flux_base_on_T2O`, `K_f·p·[O][V_O] − K_r·[OT]²`, is one such difference.
   - Variables whose Jacobian blocks are far from 1 even after scaling.

   That is my best explanation for why `electron_concentration_dry`'s floor in desorption, about 4e-5, is far above eps·‖x‖. I have not instrumented it to confirm.

2. **Starting with the user-specified version.** Agreed, and the data backs the choice. Picking the four values was empirical. I used the floors seen in the earlier sweeps, and the first two trial configurations still failed in `trapping_calibrated` until `electron_concentration_wet` got its own tolerance. An automatic floor would remove that tuning, but I would want to show that a cheap measure predicts the floor before relying on it.

# Creating a MOOSE issue

MOOSE issues follow the forms in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`. `gh issue create` bypasses those
forms, so reproduce their section headings and labels in the issue body yourself. Read the
template files before drafting; they are the source for the headings and labels below, and they
win if they have changed.

## Step 1 - Check for an existing issue

Search open and closed issues for the same subject (`gh issue list -R idaholab/moose --search
'<terms>' --state all`). If one already covers it, return its number instead of filing a
duplicate.

## Step 2 - Pick the template

- `feature-request.yml` ("Feature or Enhancement Request", label `T: task`): new capability,
  enhancement, refactor, changed default, cleanup, or documentation work. Most issues filed
  alongside a pull request are this kind.
- `bug-report.yml` ("Bug Report", labels `T: defect` and `P: normal`): existing behavior is
  wrong and can be reproduced. A missing feature is not a bug.
- Questions go to GitHub Discussions, not issues.

## Step 3 - Draft the body

Use the template's field labels as `###` headings, in the template's order, and fill every
required field. The form's optional diagnostics field may be omitted.

Feature request:

```
### Motivation

### Design

### Impact
```

Bug report:

```
### Bug Description

### Steps to Reproduce

### Impact
```

Write the content under the contribution-material rules in AGENTS.md section 9: lead with the
problem and why it matters, keep it concise, preserve exact class, parameter, and command names,
and state numbers a reader can check. Under Impact, say whether existing APIs, defaults, or input
syntax change.

Add a component label (`C: <Area>`, e.g. `C: TestHarness`, `C: Modules/Heat Transfer`) when the
area is clear; list existing labels with `gh label list -R idaholab/moose --limit 300`.

## Step 4 - Approval, then publication

Show the title, labels, and body, and wait for explicit approval before creating the issue. Then
create it with every label from the template plus the component label:

```bash
gh issue create -R idaholab/moose --title '<title>' --label 'T: task' --label 'C: <Area>' \
  --body-file <file>
```

Return the issue URL. When the issue backs a commit or pull request, reference it as `Refs #<n>`
or `Closes #<n>` there.

content.text: No existing issue covers this; #15475 is a different, closed request. Here is the draft:

input.content:
### Motivation

`ReferenceResidualConvergence` compares the residual norm of each variable against one `nl_abs_tol`. A residual cannot drop below a round-off floor, and the floor scales with the magnitude of that variable's solution and Jacobian block. When the floors of variables differ by many orders of magnitude, no single `nl_abs_tol` works for all of them:

- If `nl_abs_tol` is below the floor of some variable, Newton stagnates at that floor and the time step is cut back to `dtmin`.
- If `nl_abs_tol` is above the floor of every variable, it is far looser than needed for the variables with small floors.

TMAP8 validation case val-2g has this problem. It has eight variables. With PETSc 3.26, MOOSE's convergence check now decides convergence of `vinewtonrsls` solves. The oxygen vacancy residuals stagnate near 2e-6 and `electron_concentration_dry` stagnates near 4e-5, while the other variables converge below 1e-8. The only single tolerance that lets every solve finish is 3e-4.

### Design

Add a `variable_nl_abs_tol` parameter to `ReferenceResidualInterface`, so that both `ReferenceResidualConvergence` and `ReferenceResidualProblem` accept it. The parameter is a map from variable name to absolute tolerance, for example `variable_nl_abs_tol = 'u 1e-4 v 1e-8'`.

- A listed variable is checked against its own tolerance in place of `nl_abs_tol`.
- A variable that is not listed uses `nl_abs_tol`.
- All variables in a group of `group_variables` must have the same tolerance, because the check uses one residual norm for each group.
- `acceptable_multiplier` scales these tolerances in the same way that it scales `nl_abs_tol`.
- An unknown variable name or a negative tolerance is an input error.

### Impact

This adds one optional parameter. It does not change existing parameters, defaults, or results. Applications with variables of very different magnitudes can then converge each variable to a tolerance that fits its own floor.

- A variable that is not listed uses `nl_abs_tol`.
- All variables in a group of `group_variables` must have the same tolerance, because the check uses one residual norm for each group.
- `acceptable_multiplier` scales these tolerances in the same way that it scales `nl_abs_tol`.
- An unknown variable name or a negative tolerance is an input error.

This adds one optional parameter. It does not change existing parameters, defaults, or results. Applications with variables of very different magnitudes can then converge each variable to a tolerance that fits its own floor.

Add a `variable_nl_abs_tol` parameter to `ReferenceResidualInterface`, so that both `ReferenceResidualConvergence` and `ReferenceResidualProblem` accept it. The parameter is a map from variable name to absolute tolerance, for example `variable_nl_abs_tol = 'u 1e-4 v 1e-8'`.

- A variable that is not listed uses `nl_abs_tol`.


After you approve, I'll:
1. Create the issue.
2. Change the MOOSE commit to `refs #<new>`.
3. Push `fix-heavy-val-2d-2g` and open it as a draft stopgap PR on TMAP8.
4. Push the MOOSE branch and open a draft PR.
5. Open the val-2g follow-on as a draft TMAP8 PR that depends on both.

**Answers to your questions**

1. **Separate failure and regold commits.** Yes, TMAP8's `AGENTS.md` says: "If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately". I followed it literally. I agree it hurts `git bisect`: the failure commit is red on purpose, so bisect has to skip it, and a regression can hide behind it. A better rule would keep the input change and the regold in one green commit and put the error text in its message, if the goal is a record. Changing a project rule is your call. I can draft that change to `AGENTS.md`, or squash the commit pairs on these branches before pushing.
2. **PSS** stands for Parallel Subset Simulation. It's a Monte Carlo method from the stochastic tools module for rare-event and optimization studies. In val-2g, `val-2g_pss_optimization` runs it over the trapping parameters, using `val-2g_trapping.i` as the sub-app.
3. **Dedicated issue.** The draft is above and waits on your approval.
4. **Stopgap plus follow-on PR.** Yes. That's steps 3 and 5 of the plan above.
5. **Brittle-numerics skill updates.** Three lessons from this session would help:
   - **Round-off floors under convergence checks.** A per-variable convergence check exposes each variable's round-off floor. A stall that sits at a fixed residual for many iterations, while the reference residual stays put, means the tolerance is below that floor, not that the problem is ill-conditioned. Read the floor off the stalled iterations: compare each variable's last two residuals.
   - **The floor can move between variables.** Check it over the whole run, not only at the first failure. In val-2g the binding variable changed from vacancy to electron during desorption.
   - **Upstream changes in which code decides convergence.** A dependency can change which test decides convergence without changing any numbers. Here, PETSc 3.26 started honoring MOOSE's test. Check for that before suspecting conditioning.

   I'd add the first as a step-3 sub-case and the other two as short notes. Tell me if you want that edit.
6. **"residual" → "floor".** Done in `ReferenceResidualConvergence.md`. That sentence also appears in the issue draft above, where it already reads "floor".
7. **Map instead of a vector.** Yes, that's the main reason. Most variables have no special floor, so omitted entries should fall back to `nl_abs_tol`. A vector whose length matches the variables would force every variable to be listed. A vector over groups would also tie the input to group ordering, which is implicit when `group_variables` isn't set. Naming the variable makes the input self-describing and lets the code check unknown names.
8. **The code comment.** Done: it now says "...from variable_nl_abs_tol if given, else the generic absolute tolerance".
9. **`acceptable_multiplier`.** It isn't just a looser tolerance. The looser check applies only after `acceptable_iterations` iterations: before then, a solve must meet the tight tolerances. Once that many iterations have run, it accepts the solve if it meets the multiplied tolerances. The idea is to aim tight, but not throw away a step that is nearly converged and stalling. With `acceptable_iterations = 0`, it is the same as setting looser tolerances directly. So its purpose is close to what per-variable floors now handle more precisely, and I kept it only for consistency with `nl_abs_tol`.
10. **`nl_rel_tol = 0`.** Done. All six new tests and the other 45 reference-residual tests still pass, and the gold file is unchanged.

Refs #476

This PR fixes the six heavy-test failures on `devel` (for example https://civet.inl.gov/job/4323472/). They started with the MOOSE submodule update to PETSc 3.26. MOOSE's `ReferenceResidualConvergence` now decides convergence of `vinewtonrsls` solves and checks each variable separately. The heavy val-2d and val-2g solves then stagnate at round-off floors below their absolute tolerances, and the time step is cut back to `dtmin`.

- val-2d: `nl_abs_tol = 1e-9` moves from the light test `cli_args` into `val-2d.i`, so the heavy test uses it too. The output matches the existing gold.
- val-2g: `nl_abs_tol` rises from 1e-10 to 3e-4. In a sweep over the three heavy cases, 3e-5 and smaller still stagnate, while 1e-4 to 1e-3 finish. 3e-4 is about ten times above the largest observed floor. The heavy CSV gold files are regolded. Values change by less than 3e-3 relative, except `recombination_flux_T2_wet_left` at the first output step, which changes by 22%. That value is the same for every tolerance from 1e-4 to 1e-3, so the new value is the converged one.

This is a stopgap. A single tolerance of 3e-4 is far looser than six of the eight val-2g variables need. A follow-on PR switches val-2g to per-variable absolute tolerances from idaholab/moose#34305.

# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Ask the user if you need to load a MOOSE conda environment, and if so, what the name of the conda environment is
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
- Use `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` to validate before committing
- Use `./tmap8-opt -i <file>.i` to run input files
- Write parameter values in the units the reference source used; use the MOOSE units system for conversion — the units system is self-documenting and does not require inline comments
- State the unit system at the top of every input file in a comment block

## Testing
- Run tests only when `.C`, `.h`, or `test/tests/` files change
- Run only the affected module: `./run_tests -j<N> --re <module>`

## Session log
- Every session must be associated with a GitHub issue on `idaholab/TMAP8`; ask the user for the issue number at the start of the session if one is not provided, or create one if the user instructs you to
- **SQA requirement:** When creating a GitHub issue with `gh`, you must use the appropriate template from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`; read the available templates first, select the one that fits (e.g. `bug-report.md` for bugs, `feature-request.md` for new features or tasks), and populate all sections in the template body — passing a bare description without following the template structure is not acceptable
- Before committing, copy the current session's `.jsonl` file into `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/`. For Claude Code sessions the file is the most recently modified `.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/`; for Codex sessions check the equivalent Codex session directory. Do not remove old session files already in that directory — append the new one alongside them.

## Committing
- Commit at minimum after: every input file that successfully runs, every test that passes or fails, and every new class added
- If a test or run failed, commit the failure state first (include the full error message in the commit body), then commit the fix separately
- Every commit must reference the associated GitHub issue (e.g. `Refs #<issue-number>` or `Closes #<issue-number>` as appropriate) in the commit message
- **Every commit must include an updated copy of the session `.jsonl`** — before staging, copy the current session file from `~/.claude/projects/<repo-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` to `doc/content/agent/<issue-number>/` and stage it; this is a critical SQA requirement. Do not remove session files already present in that directory — if multiple Claude/Codex sessions contribute to the same branch and issue, all session files must be kept.
- Every commit must include these trailers:
```
Refs #<issue-number>
AI-assisted: true
AI-model: <model name>
AI-version: <model version>
Co-Authored-By: <model name> <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

## Pull requests
- If the linked issue already contains a complete Reason/Design/Impact description, the PR body should contain only the closing reference (e.g. `Closes #<issue-number>`) — do not duplicate the issue content or leave template sections empty
- If the PR introduces physics/modeling decisions, non-obvious AI reasoning, or tests not described in the issue, add those as a short addendum below the issue reference
- Never merge autonomously

## Never do
- Modify existing passing tests without explicit user instruction
- Modify the build system without explicit user instruction
- Make physics modeling decisions without flagging them to the user
- Suppress or bypass test failures
